 Keep calm and K on: How Korea became Indian brands favourite marketing ingredient
 Part fandom, part flavour and fully commerce, the Korean wave is giving marketers plenty to be K-ontent about
 By   Anuja Jain | November 1, 2026, 15:03:49 IST Share Share this Article
 × WhatsApp Facebook Twitter Linkedin Mail 
 Follow Us 
 The significance goes beyond convenience. For international trends, commerce platforms can become discovery and testing environments, letting consumers find products that earlier had limited visibility or distribution in India. In India, for years, aspirational marketing has been scripted through Western allusions, American accent, and references to either London or New York. However, the script is changing in Hangul. As per the recent Ormax studies, 107.8 million Indians watch K-Dramas on the very least once every month as against the previous figure of 72.9 million viewers in 2025. The growth of 48 percent in one year is unprecedented for most content types in the country.
 Brands have noticed. McDonald’s has roped in global icon G-Dragon, Zepto has built a Korean street in Delhi, and Netflix has put WWE legend The Great Khali in a pink onesie to sell heartbreak. What looks like a string of quirky campaigns is a larger shift. Korean storytelling has moved from a niche fandom to a mainstream cultural currency, and marketers are racing to speak it fluently.
 The audience is far wider than the stereotype 
 The natural inclination would be to assume that those who watch K-dramas make up a narrow, urban, and premium streaming audience. However, the Ormax numbers suggest otherwise. In India, 45 per cent of K-drama viewers are connected TV viewers, whereas 58 per cent of the K-drama viewers in India are AVOD viewers, which means that they view ad-supported video content without paying for the premium streaming service.

While 23 per cent of female OTT audiences in India watch K-dramas, the figure among male OTT audiences is 11 per cent. Women make up 60 per cent of the overall K-drama audience, the highest female share among the content formats Ormax tracks. The format is also climbing the charts. In 2026 so far, eight K-dramas across Netflix, Amazon MX Player, Amazon Prime Video and JioHotstar have appeared in Ormax StreamView’s weekly Top 50 most-watched properties on OTT in India. 
 It is no accident that the format travels so well. The commercial trajectory was visible by the 2010s, when Korean drama exports generated US$167 million in 2013, four times the value recorded a decade earlier. By 2015, Korean drama broadcast licences were being sold across non-Asian markets, with the United States accounting for 4,291 titles, according to the research. The same research traces this rise to policy and institutional changes in South Korea in the late 1990s, when cultural industries came to be treated as strategic contributors to economic growth. India is now seeing the downstream effect of a strategy that was decades in the making.
 From screen to shelf in ten minutes 
 If K-dramas create desire, quick commerce collapses the distance to purchase. Ritika Taneja, Senior Vice President, E-commerce, WPP Media, points to Korean culture as an example of how commerce can shorten the gap between cultural discovery and consumption. A consumer may encounter Korean food through entertainment and then find ramen on a 10-minute delivery platform.
 The significance goes beyond convenience. For international trends, commerce platforms can become discovery and testing environments, letting consumers find products that earlier had limited visibility or distribution in India. For brands, those transactions can also signal demand before they commit to wider expansion. That is where the K-drama phenomenon starts looking less like a content story and more like a commerce story.
 Zepto’s own numbers make the case. The platform recorded more than 4.6 lakh ramen searches and over 1 lakh Korean noodle searches, the backdrop to Seoul Street, an invite-only immersive event in Delhi that recreated a Korean street with food, music, fandom and interactive experiences.
 “Zepto’s brand playbook has always been about culture hacking, identifying what people already love and creating new ways for them to experience it,” said Chandan Mendiratta, Chief Brand Officer, Zepto. “With Seoul Street, we saw a natural connection between Korean and Indian culture, particularly our shared love for food, family, music and community. The growing popularity of Korean food in India, from ramyun and snacks to sauces, showed us how deeply this interest has moved beyond screens.”
 Mass brands go Korean, on purpose 
 Mass marketing cannot afford to stand aside, as the McDonald’s India North & East has started its Asia Chicken Campaign in collaboration with 13 different Asian countries. It has partnered with G-Dragon in a strategic association referred to as ICON X ICON, marking the increasing popularity of Korean culture across the globe. The core of this marketing campaign is the Gochujang Butter Sauce, which is an innovative K-Flavour created by McDonald’s Korea. It is inspired by jangs, or fermented sauces, of Korea and combines the savory flavors of gochujang and butter, providing you with mild spiciness and rich flavor.
 The business logic is audience driven. Sushmita Kashyap, Director, Integrated Marketing, Corporate Communications and Strategy at McDonald’s India, notes that Gen Z accounts for 45 per cent of total quick service restaurant consumption, the biggest cohort in every band of going out. The Korean range is built to meet them at different price points. “Korean is layered,” she said. “People can choose what fits with respect to taste and also the pricing. So we make a democratic impact.” Spicy offerings sit at a slightly premium tier, while value options deliver surprise at the lower end.
 However, Netflix went with comedy. Their Indian team featured The Great Khali in a pink polka dotted onesie with a bow, photographed in a pink Korean-themed room filled with fairy lights and stuffed animals. He does the finger heart gesture common in Korea, turns the pages of a scrapbook of K-drama movies, and eats Ramen while crying into tissue as he watches the movie When Life Gives You Tangerines. “K-Paglu with a Capital K” was the caption used. This is obviously a reference joke, which works only when the audience knows what it is all about.
 Where the K-Wave heads next 
 The common trend seen in these marketing initiatives is the same. Entertainment creates the fan base, commerce grabs the first sale, and brand scales up the taste for all. The takeaway for marketers here is that the relevance cannot be achieved merely by adopting the western trends any more. With a female base of 60 per cent, AVOD viewership of 58 per cent and a rapidly growing monthly viewer count, Korean wave has much to offer that other trends fail to deliver. It is only those brands which see it as an enduring consumption shift than a mere hashtag campaign that will be able to spice up the conversation in the next wave.
